Perhaps I might say a few words now about harbours and rivers engineering projects. The use of model studies, in conjunction with the national research council, was increased and emphasized to study proposed projects in advance with a view to determining the results which can be expected and minimizing the possibility of inefficient and expensive undertakings which fail to achieve the desired results. Among the projects which have special problems and have therefore been subject to prior model study are the ones at Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, which as we all know has been a very tough problem; Saint John and Ingalls Head, New Brunswick; Glace Bay, Nova Scotia; Chandler and Matane, Quebec. A model study of the Fraser river development has been in use for some years.
To turn to development engineering projects, which come under another branch of the department, during the last year work on the construction of the trans-Canada highway through the national parks included completion of the bituminous stabilized base course in Banff and Yoho national parks, making it possible now to drive from the east gate at Banff to the western boundary of Yoho on a first-class paved highway. I might add that it is possible to drive on a first-class paved trans-Canada highway from
Supply-Public Works
the western border of Yoho park all the way to Kenora, Ontario. I did it myself the summer before last and the highway is even better now.
In Glacier and Revelstoke national parks the start of construction was delayed in that the route involving these parks was not decided upon until 1956. As members from the west will know, the decision then taken was to abandon the Big Bend route around the bend of the Columbia and build a new road paralleling the Canadian Pacific railway from Golden to Revelstoke with the exception that the road goes through Rogers pass and the railroad goes through a five mile tunnel having abandoned the road through the pass quite a few years ago.
Similarly, in the case of Terra Nova in Newfoundland this park was only declared in 1957. However, the work in these three parks has been pressed forward and all of the trans-Canada highway mileage was under grading contract by last summer. In Terra Nova in particular, while grading is not yet completed traffic is making use of the road. A full statement of activities on the trans-Canada highway through the provinces was given during the readings of the bill to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act last March. However, an indication of the accelerated progress on this undertaking on the basis of final figures for 1958-59 is that Canada's share of expenditures for the year rose to over $51 million, as I pointed out earlier in my remarks, which exceeded the original estimate by an appreciable amount.
Other projects in the field of highways and bridges which concerned the department during the year included the awarding of contracts for the substructures of bridges at Campbellton, New Brunswick, which will run to Cross Point, Quebec, $1,261,600, and at Burlington, Ontario, $698,300. In addition, the contract for the superstructure of the Burlington bridge has been let at an amount of $3,684,400 and tenders for the Campbell-ton-Cross Point superstructure have been called for June 4.
Work on behalf of other government departments was undertaken in all major fields of activity of the department. More than 200 individual projects were undertaken for 15 other departments. The majority of these were on behalf of the R.C.M.P. and northern affairs and national resources and included are major developments which are taking place in northern communities. There was also a heavy program of highway construction and location undertaken for northern affairs and national resources. In the national parks some of the principal items were reconstruction of the Banff-Jasper and Banff-Windermere highways and the Emerald lake

Supply-Public Works
road in the west and of the Cabot trail and the gulf shore road in the east.
In the northwest territories the extension of the Mackenzie highway toward Yellowknife was continued both on the location and construction sides. Other road survey projects in these areas include the Marian river road, the Fort Fitzgerald-Bell Rock road and a road from Peace Point westerly in Wood Buffalo park. In the Yukon territory, the reconnaissance survey of the road from the Dawson-Stewart highway to the oil reserves in the Peal plateau and thence to Fort McPherson, a distance of about 300 miles, was completed, as was the final location of the first 140 miles of the road. During the past winter a clearing contract was awarded on the first 45 miles where construction will start this summer. All of these undertakings involved an expenditure of $12 million during 1958-59 with the money being provided in the appropriation of northern affairs and natural resources.
So much for a brief review of the fiscal year 1958-59. I should now like to give members of the committee a few of the highlights of the departmental program for 1959-60. The total amount requested, exclusive of statutory items, in the 1959-60 estimates is $173.6 million. This reflects a decrease of $17.8 million on ordinary account. The decrease relates mainly to the completion of the major construction phases on a number of construction projects, for example, the customs building and post office at St. John's, Newfoundland, the national revenue building at Montreal, buildings for mines and technical surveys here in Ottawa and also some very expensive harbour improvements such as at Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, and Toronto. I hope, by the way, that we are not going to be criticized for reducing our estimate by a small amount.
Offsetting the decrease to some extent are additional requirements for the Campbellton-Cross Point bridge, an increase of $1,800,000, the low level Burlington canal bridge, an increase of $2,200,000, and an increased requirement related to the construction of a new dredge for the west coast dredging fleet, the increase being $660,000. Additional expenditure of about $1 million is included for the construction of the trans-Canada highway in the national parks. An increase of $3 million is also forecast in the contribution to the provinces for the trans-Canada highway, although this is a statutory item.
As for the winter employment implications of the 1959-60 estimates, although the amount provided for repairs, upkeep and normal maintenance of public buildings across the country is slightly reduced, it is the intention again to schedule these works to be carried out during the winter months in the interest of relieving seasonal unemployment. The department's activities in this field in

In so far as the development engineering projects are concerned for 1959-60 fiscal year, slope seeding-as hon. members know that is where you spray grass seed on the slopes of the highway-general clean-up and the installation of guard railing will be carried out along the paved highway in Banff and Yoho parks. The grade separation at the Norquay overpass in Banff, as well as the Wapta lake railway relocation in Yoho, will be completed. All aggregate needed for the final paving of the trans-Canada hghway in those two parks will be crushed. In Glacier and Revelstoke parks, depending upon weather conditions, the major part of the grading of the highway will be completed as will most of the structures. Avalanche studies in the Rogers pass section of Glacier and the design of suitable avalanche defences for this area will be continued. In Terra Nova park grading on the highway will be completed and we will be in a position to proceed with the bituminous stabilized base course. For all of these projects, an amount of $13,400,000 is provided. However, if we encounter a good construction season, it is possible that a supplementary appropriation will be needed later in the year. An amount of $48 million is included in these estimates to cover payments to the provinces under the trans-Canada agreements during 1959-60.
In the few minutes which remain, I should like to give to the members a sketch of the situation with regard to five or six particular projects. One of the most challenging and most interesting projects the department has under construction is the improvement of the harbour in St. John's Newfoundland. A further amount of one and one-quarter million dollars toward harbour improvements in St. John's, Newfoundland is included in this year's estimates. This will provide funds to allow a continuation of the major reconstruction program for this port for which funds were provided in last year's estimates. This is one of the largest projects which the department has undertaken, with the total cost being in the neighbourhood of $13 million. To date, three contracts totalling over a million dollars have been awarded to provide a marine [The Deputy Chairman.]

agency wharf for use of the Department of Transport, a small boat basin and a significant quantity of dredging. The first of the demolition work contracts has been advertised, with more to follow.
It is expected that tenders will be called in July or August for the main finger pier and the related operating facilities, with this particular contract representing a value of probably some six to seven million dollars. There are numerous portions of this harbour development which are receiving continued study at present, as the planning is relatively involved. I refer to improvement in the road traffic surrounding the waterfront; the extension of sewers through the new waterfront structures; naval and Canadian National Railways' installations; and such other problems. A large number of properties, including some private homes, wholesale and retail businesses, lumber concerns and a fish plant are being acquired in order to make these improvements possible.
The need for modernization of St. John's harbour is easily seen by a comparison of the cargo handling costs there and in other Canadian harbours. The capital expenditures being made in connection with this development will pay for themselves in the savings to be realized by Newfoundland through the improved handling and distribution of cargo. The plan includes, in addition to the works now under way and the large finger pier- it is so named because it is shaped like a finger-an adjacent marginal wharf which will provide berthage for all sizes and types of ships using this harbour. Transit sheds, storage sheds, etc., are of course included.
Progress on the general project has been favourable. However, I expect the work will not be completed until 1962 or 1963. This project is, of course, supplying much needed employment for the St. John's area and when the main pier contract is awarded this employment will be greatly increased and should be of particular help during the coming winter.
Hon. members will have heard about the possibility of a causeway from New Brunswick to Prince Edward Island over the Northumberland strait. As reported to the house, the government has undertaken a feasibility study for providing a crossing over Northumberland strait to replace the existing rail and highway ferry service. Proposals for such a crossing had dated back to 1891. The most recent proposal was put forward by the province of Prince Edward Island in 1956, when they suggested that a rock-filled causeway be constructed at a cost of $50 million, and asked the federal government to investigate rock sources on cape Tormentine. Preliminary work was done on this, as well

as an economic study of the cost of operations and capitalization of the existing ferry system.
The difficulty in considering the proposal of Prince Edward Island, as well as previous ones, was that no engineering studies had ever been made to establish that a causeway could be constructed and supported by sufficient data to give an estimate of cost. Most important, investigations had not been made to establish what would be the results of tidal conditions along the coast should such a causeway be constructed. As this information was required before a proper assessment of either the physical or economic feasibility of the project could be considered, the government authorized the undertaking of this study in March 1958.
The study has been most complex. The design of any type of structure required a complete tidal survey throughout the whole of Northumberland strait. This work was undertaken by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys which had engaged a boat to put the work in hand by May, 1958. In addition to establishing the existing tidal conditions, that department predicted the changes in tidal conditions which would result from the construction of a causeway. It was established that a causeway would completely change the phases of the tide at the crossing, so that high tide on one side of the crossing would coincide with low tide on the other side, creating a condition where there would be up to ten feet differential in head on opposite sides of the causeway. It was also established that such a causeway would create changes in tidal ranges to varying degrees along both coasts of Northumberland strait. This necessitated a survey of existing shore line conditions and land use along the coasts of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island in the Northumberland straight area and these surveys are now being used to establish estimates of cost of remedial works and possible land damage as a result of construction of a causeway.
In addition, it was necessary to have a very complete survey of the ice conditions in the strait and predict what the conditions would be as a result of causeway construction as obviously any change in these conditions would require careful study in relation to navigation and fisheries.
A great deal of credit is due to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys for their tidal studies and for their studies on the shoreline and land use, particularly in view of the fact that they were able to undertake this work so efficiently during 1958 and provided so much information in a limited time.
Considering the scope of the study and the fact that each phase of the survey was, to
Supply-Public Works
some degree, dependent on the information from other phases, the work has progressed remarkably well and it was possible to provide sufficient information to the consultants who were responsible for the site investigation and preparation of alternate designs enabling them to submit their report within the last week.
The alternatives in this report will now be considered by this department as well as by other departments concerned, such as transport, the Canadian National Railways and fisheries, and will be consolidated with the reports on the cost of remedial works and possible land damage. This review is now proceeding, following which the government will give consideration to the economic feasibility of the project.
